item.title: United States Seeks Mexico’s Review of Alleged Denial of Workers’ Rights at Madobox
item.description:
United States Seeks Mexico’s Review of Alleged Denial of Workers’ Rights at Madobox pbrouillette Mon, 11/02/2026 - 15:27

WASHINGTON — The Office of the United States Trade Representative has invoked the Rapid Response Labor Mechanism (RRM) in the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA) to review whether workers at Madobox, S.A. de C.V. (Madobox), located in the city of Uruapan in the state of Michoacán, Mexico, are being denied the right to freedom of association and collective bargaining. The U.S. request for review follows an RRM petition received from a Mexican labor union alleging that Madobox is interfering with union activity at the facility. The United States has suspended liquidation of unliquidated entries of goods from the Madobox facility, which produces boxes for commercial use.

Background

The United States Trade Representative (Trade Representative) and the Secretary of Labor co-chair the Interagency Labor Committee for Monitoring and Enforcement (ILC). On September 30, 2026, the Sindicato Nacional de Trabajadores y Empleados de la Industria del Comercio, Alimenticia, Textil, Automotriz, Metalúrgica, Servicios y Distribución “Generalísimo José María Morelos y Pavón”—a Mexican labor union affiliated with the Confederacion Central Nacional (COCENA)—filed a Rapid Response Mechanism (RRM) petition alleging a denial of rights at Madobox. The petition alleges that Madobox is interfering with union activity at the facility, including by unlawfully arranging a collective bargaining agreement (CBA) that was negotiated without workers, by coercing and misinforming workers about the CBA and their union rights, and by unlawfully dismissing workers in retaliation for union activity. The ILC reviews RRM petitions that it receives, and the accompanying information, within 30 days.

After conducting this review, the ILC determined that there is sufficient, credible evidence of a denial of rights enabling the good faith invocation of enforcement mechanisms under the USMCA. As a result, the Trade Representative has submitted a request to Mexico under Annex 31-A of the USMCA that Mexico review whether workers at Madobox are being denied the right to freedom of association and collective bargaining. The Trade Representative has also directed the Secretary of the Treasury to suspend liquidation of unliquidated entries of goods from Madobox.  

Mexico has 10 days to agree to conduct a review and, if it agrees, 45 days from today to complete the review.  

A copy of the request for review can be found here.

A copy of the letter to the Secretary of the Treasury can be found here.

Information about previous requests can be found here.

item.title: United States and Mexico Announce Memorandum of Understanding at Industrias Tecnos Facility
item.description:
United States and Mexico Announce Memorandum of Understanding at Industrias Tecnos Facility pbrouillette Mon, 11/02/2026 - 15:13

WASHINGTON — The United States and Mexico announced today a memorandum of understanding regarding denial of rights concerns at the Industrias Tecnos, S.A. de C.V. (Industrias Tecnos or the company) facility located in Cuernavaca, Morelos, Mexico, where the company manufactures small arms ammunition.  

The memorandum of understanding details a plan to remedy violations of Mexican law at the facility and includes actions aimed at ensuring freedom of association and collective bargaining rights are protected at the facility moving forward.

Under the terms of the memorandum of understanding, the Government of Mexico (Mexico) will ensure that Industrias Tecnos takes various remedial actions, including to:

  • Verify proper compensation for dismissed workers as required by Mexican law, for any wages or benefits those workers did not receive as a result of unlawful dismissals;
  • Implement and train all company personnel on a neutrality statement and guidelines related to the freedom of association and collective bargaining, including a zero-tolerance policy for violations, and commit to additional retraining as needed; 
  • Install and publicize a complaint mechanism through which workers can report violations of their rights and breaches of company policies anonymously and confidentially; and
  • Maintain on the company website and in any internal communications platform the neutrality statement and guidelines, training materials, and information about complaint mechanisms maintained by the company and Mexico, such that the information is easily accessible to workers.

Under the terms of the memorandum of understanding, Mexico will, among other actions:

  • Review and verify determinations made in relation to dismissed workers identified by the United States to ensure outcomes were effectuated in accordance with Mexican law;
  • Monitor the facility with regard to the obligations of the memorandum of understanding and compliance with Mexican laws related to freedom of association and collective bargaining; 
  • Conduct in-person training that is structured to ensure all workers understand their right to freedom of association and collective bargaining and how to exercise it;
  • Conduct separate workers’ rights training for supervisors, human resources and labor relations personnel, and other high-level and “trusted” officials; and
  • Maintain a direct email address, reporting platform, and telephone line for workers to anonymously report any potential acts of unlawful interference or other violations of freedom of association and collective bargaining rights, and timely investigate any allegations.

The United States and Mexico agreed to establish a deadline of October 15, 2026, to complete the actions listed in the memorandum of understanding.

Background

The United States Trade Representative and the Secretary of Labor co-chair the Interagency Labor Committee for Monitoring and Enforcement (ILC). On May 23, 2024, the ILC received a Rapid Response Labor Mechanism (RRM) petition from Sindicato Independiente de Trabajadores y Empleados, Transporte, Carga y Descarga, Exploración y Explotación de Minerales Básicos, Productos Metálicos, Similares y Conexos de la República Mexicana (Sindicato Metálico), a Mexican labor union. The petition alleged an ongoing Denial of Rights by Industrias Tecnos at its facility in Morelos, Mexico. The ILC reviews RRM petitions that it receives, and the accompanying information, within 30 days. The ILC determined that there was sufficient, credible evidence of a denial of rights enabling the good faith invocation of enforcement mechanisms.    

As a result, on June 24, 2024, the United States submitted a request that Mexico review the matter, and Mexico thereafter agreed to conduct a review. After Mexico issued a report finding no Denial of Rights at the facility, the United States requested the establishment of a panel pursuant to Article 31-A.5.1(a) of the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement.  

Read the full memorandum of understanding here.

item.title: Ambassador Greer Issues Statement on President Trump’s Intent to Terminate Rwanda and South Africa from the AGOA Trade Preference Program
item.description:
Ambassador Greer Issues Statement on President Trump’s Intent to Terminate Rwanda and South Africa from the AGOA Trade Preference Program myarbrough Mon, 11/02/2026 - 11:41

WASHINGTON — Today, Ambassador Jamieson Greer issued a statement following President Trump notifying Congress and the governments of Rwanda and South Africa of his intent to terminate these countries from the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA) trade preference program, as of January 1, 2027.

“The Office of the United States Trade Representative led the annual interagency review of sub-Saharan African countries’ eligibility for the AGOA trade preference program. Based on the review, President Trump found that the governments of Rwanda and South Africa are engaging in practices that are inconsistent with AGOA’s eligibility criteria,” said Ambassador Greer. “These concerning and pervasive practices include, but are not limited to, barriers that undermine American trade and investment and practices that pose a threat to U.S. national security and foreign policy interests in the region. The Trump Administration is working to ensure our African partners take the necessary steps to meet the eligibility criteria.”

Background:

In Rwanda, the Trump Administration is deeply concerned by the following issues: trade and investment barriers, rule of law, political pluralism, internationally recognized worker rights, human rights, and threats to U.S. national security and foreign policy interests. In South Africa, the Trump Administration is deeply concerned by barriers to U.S. trade and investment, corruption, and threats to U.S. national security and foreign policy interests.

item.title: America First Seafood Strategy Charts Course to Restoring U.S. Seafood Dominance
item.description:
America First Seafood Strategy Charts Course to Restoring U.S. Seafood Dominance myarbrough Wed, 10/28/2026 - 09:39

WASHINGTON – In honor of National Seafood Month, the White House unveiled the historic America First Seafood Strategy, outlining a whole-of-government approach to revitalize the U.S. fishing industry by removing foreign trade barriers and unlocking new markets for U.S. fishermen. Under President Trump’s leadership, U.S. seafood exports reached $5.53 billion in 2025, increasing 12% compared to 2024, and many of our trading partners have committed to remove trade barriers that undercut our global competitiveness. U.S. seafood exports are continuing to trend upwards in 2026.

REELING IN THE WINS: The Trump Administration continues to secure new and enforce existing commitments from key trading partners to combat illegal, unreported, and unregulated (IUU) fishing, prevent forced labor on the high seas, and address harmful fisheries subsidies and other practices that distort markets and decimate the U.S. seafood industry.

  • Taiwan committed to ensure that its fisheries subsidies do not contribute to overcapacity and overfishing and address violations of internationally recognized labor rights on board commercial fishing vessels. Read the Agreement on Reciprocal Trade with Taiwan here.
  • Argentina, Bangladesh, Ecuador, and Indonesia committed to combat IUU fishing, deter trade in IUU fishing-derived products, and address harmful fisheries subsidies through the use of robust fisheries management regimes. Read the Agreements on Reciprocal Trade with those countries here. 
  • USTR continues to engage and closely monitor Mexico’s implementation of its United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA) fisheries-related environmental obligations, including its commitments to prevent illegal fishing in the Upper Gulf of California.

FOREIGN TRADE PRACTICES PUT AMERICAN FISHERMEN ON THE HOOK: The United States is a global leader in responsibly managed fisheries and sustainable seafood — U.S. fisheries are scientifically monitored and legally enforced under 10 national standards of sustainability. Illegally caught and heavily subsidized foreign seafood, including seafood caught using forced labor on fishing vessels, are undercutting American fishermen that play by the rules. 

Every year, global losses from IUU fishing reach an estimated $50 billion with U.S. industry absorbing a major portion of that financial burden. In the America First Seafood Strategy, USTR spotlighted foreign trade barriers and distortive subsidies that continue to limit opportunities for U.S. seafood producers in key export markets.

  • Japan imposes tariffs of up to 10% and enforces import quotas that disadvantage American exporters relative to competitors that benefit from preferential market access.
  • The EU CATCH scheme imposes burdensome documentation and reporting requirements on U.S. fishermen despite the United States’ strong fisheries management and enforcement regime and safeguards against IUU fishing.
  • India’s substantial fisheries subsidy program and Vietnam’s IUU fishing practices directly impact U.S. fishermen and supply chains, exporting seafood to the United States at lower-than-market prices.

PUTTING AMERICAN FISHERMEN FIRST: President Trump’s trade policies will continue to expand market access for the 8.4 billion pounds of U.S. caught seafood each year and protect the 1.7 million jobs supported by America’s seafood industry.

  • The future of seafood in the United States will be built by American fishermen, American workers, and American industry—not illegally-caught and heavily-subsidized foreign imports.
  • In collaboration with other federal agencies, USTR will continue to use negotiations and enforcement tools to open new markets for U.S. exports and remove foreign trade that distort seafood trade and disadvantage U.S. fishermen.

item.title: Ambassador Greer Issues Statement on the Status of the U.S.-EU Détente Following Record-Breaking Loan from the European Investment Bank to Airbus
item.description:
Ambassador Greer Issues Statement on the Status of the U.S.-EU Détente Following Record-Breaking Loan from the European Investment Bank to Airbus pbrouillette Mon, 10/26/2026 - 18:59

WASHINGTON — Today, Ambassador Jamieson Greer issued a statement regarding the status of the U.S.-EU deal to pause duties on certain EU imports, following a record-breaking loan from the European Investment Bank to Airbus.

“I had sincerely hoped that trade-distorting European subsidies to Airbus were a thing of the past,” said Ambassador Greer. “For decades, France, Germany, and Spain have aggressively supported Airbus, their national champion aircraft manufacturer, to gain an unfair advantage over U.S. aerospace workers and businesses. After winning at the WTO and imposing significant U.S. duties on EU imports in response, USTR struck a deal with the EU to pause those duties in exchange for a mutual commitment to provide financing to large civil aircraft (LCA) producers on market terms. Yet, this summer, almost immediately after the EU extended this pause, the European Investment Bank awarded Airbus its largest loan ever to benefit Airbus projects in France, Germany, and Spain. Despite ongoing requests, USTR still has no details about this loan. This situation injects substantial uncertainty into transatlantic trade in the aerospace sector. It is important this situation is resolved as soon as possible to ensure market-driven production in the aerospace sector and to avoid violation of the terms of our hard-won LCA deal.”

item.title: United States Announces Successful Resolution of Rapid Response Labor Mechanism Matter at Amphenol Optimize
item.description:
United States Announces Successful Resolution of Rapid Response Labor Mechanism Matter at Amphenol Optimize pbrouillette Fri, 10/23/2026 - 16:06

WASHINGTON — The United States today announced the successful resolution of the USMCA Rapid Response Labor Mechanism (RRM) matter at the Amphenol Optimize México, S.A. de C.V. (Amphenol) facility located in Nogales, Sonora, Mexico, which manufactures automotive and aerospace connectors, cables, and components. The United States and Mexico agreed on a course of remediation to address labor rights violations occurring at the facility, including employer interference in union activity and retaliatory dismissals of workers. That plan has now been implemented, and the Denial of Rights concerns raised in the U.S. request for review have been remediated. As a result, the United States Trade Representative has directed the Secretary of the Treasury to resume liquidation of unliquidated entries of goods from the facility.

Actions taken by the facility to address the matter include: 

  • Reinstating nine workers with full backpay and benefits; 
  • Implementing a neutrality statement and guidelines related to the freedom of association and collective bargaining; and
  • Installing and publicizing a complaint mechanism through which workers can report violations of their rights and breaches of company policies.

Actions taken by the Government of Mexico to address the matter include: 

  • Delivering in-person trainings for all company personnel on the freedom of association and collective bargaining; 
  • Monitoring the facility and engaging with workers and the company throughout its review period; and
  • Maintaining a direct email address, reporting platform, and telephone line for workers to anonymously report any potential acts of unlawful interference or other violations of freedom of association and collective bargaining rights, and timely investigating any allegations.

Background

The United States Trade Representative and the Secretary of Labor co-chair the Interagency Labor Committee for Monitoring and Enforcement (ILC). On April 11, 2025, the ILC received an RRM petition from the Sindicato Industrial Operaciones y Manufacturas, a Mexican labor union. The petition alleged that Amphenol had violated workers’ right to freedom of association and collective bargaining by coercing workers to vote for the company-favored outcome during a union vote, discouraging workers from joining an independent union, and taking reprisals against workers due to their union preferences, including through dismissals. The ILC reviews RRM petitions that it receives, and the accompanying information, within 30 days. The ILC determined that there was sufficient, credible evidence of a denial of rights enabling the good faith invocation of enforcement mechanisms.  
 
As a result, on May 9, 2025, the United States Trade Representative submitted a request to Mexico to review the matter. Mexico accepted the request, conducted an investigation, and worked with Amphenol to provide remediation to dismissed workers and implement facility-wide measures aimed at safeguarding freedom of association and collective bargaining rights. The United States has reviewed the matter and concluded the situation to have been remediated.  

As a result of the above actions taken by the facility and Mexico to resolve the action, the United States agrees that there is no ongoing denial of rights. Ambassador Greer’s letter directing the Secretary of the Treasury to resume liquidation of unliquidated entries of goods from the facility is available here.

Read the full course of remediation here.

Read an unofficial courtesy Spanish translation of the full course of remediation here.

Information about previous requests can be found here.

item.title: United States and Mexico Announce Course of Remediation at Minera Peñasquito
item.description:
United States and Mexico Announce Course of Remediation at Minera Peñasquito pbrouillette Fri, 10/23/2026 - 09:06

WASHINGTON — The Office of the United States Trade Representative and the Government of Mexico (Mexico) today announced a course of remediation at Minera Peñasquito, S.A. de C.V. (Newmont Peñasquito), located in the state of Zacatecas, Mexico. The remediation plan will help ensure workers at the facility can freely exercise their right to freedom of association and collective bargaining.  

Actions already taken by the company to address the matter include:  

  • Posting and dissemination of a neutrality statement and company guidelines on freedom of association and collective bargaining; and
  • Installation of a complaint mechanism for workers to report violations of their rights anonymously and confidentially.

Under the course of remediation, Mexico will ensure that Newmont Peñasquito will, among other things:

  • Reinstate and provide full backpay and benefits to two workers; 
  • Distribute hard copies of the neutrality statement and company guidelines related to freedom of association and collective bargaining to all company personnel;
  • Implement the neutrality statement and company guidelines on freedom of association and collective bargaining, including a zero-tolerance policy for violations; 
  • Publicly acknowledge, through meetings with the workers and postings at the facility, the company’s unlawful and interfering practices;
  • Conduct in-person training for all company personnel during work hours regarding rights related to freedom of association and collective bargaining; and
  • Maintain its complaint mechanism for workers to report violations of their rights anonymously and confidentially.

Under the course of remediation, Mexico will:

  • Review and facilitate the reinstatement and severance processes to ensure two workers receive reinstatement offers and full backpay and benefits, or full severance payments, as applicable; and
  • Maintain a direct email address and telephone line for workers to anonymously report any potential acts of unlawful interference or other violations of workers’ freedom of association and collective bargaining rights.

The United States and Mexico agreed to establish a deadline of October 28, 2026 to complete the course of remediation.

Background

The United States Trade Representative and the Secretary of Labor co-chair the Interagency Labor Committee for Monitoring and Enforcement (ILC). On May 13, 2026, the ILC received an RRM petition from the Sindicato Nacional de Trabajadores Mineros, Metalúrgicos, Siderúrgicos y Similares de la República Mexicana (Los Mineros), a Mexican labor union. The petition alleged that Newmont Peñasquito had violated workers’ rights by retaliating against workers for engaging in union activity, including through unlawful dismissals. The ILC reviews RRM petitions that it receives, and the accompanying information, within 30 days.

The ILC determined that there was sufficient, credible evidence of a denial of rights enabling the good faith invocation of enforcement mechanisms. As a result, the United States Trade Representative submitted a request that Mexico review whether workers at Newmont Peñasquito were being denied the right to freedom of association and collective bargaining. Mexico agreed to conduct a review. Following Mexico’s investigation, the United States and Mexico agreed on a course of remediation.

item.description:
USTR Announces 2026 Award Recipients pbrouillette Wed, 10/21/2026 - 19:05

WASHINGTON — Today, the Office of the United States Trade Representative (USTR) hosted its annual awards ceremony, celebrating the achievements and notable milestones of its staff. During the program, award recipients were announced in the following categories: Ambassador’s Award, William B. Kelly Award, Linda Enoch Award, Excellence in Service Award, Erland Herfindahl Award, Superior Achievement Award, Distinguished Career Service Award, Team Award, Way to Go Award, and Length of Service Award.

“Through their unwavering commitment to public service and pursuit of excellence, the USTR team has helped advance and execute President Trump’s America First Trade Policy, delivering lasting benefits for American farmers, manufacturers, workers, and businesses of all sizes,” said Ambassador Jamieson Greer. “Our team embodies the true meaning of public service, leading with integrity and professionalism. From our economists and legal counsel to our trade negotiators and overseas staff, I am very appreciative of your hard work and dedication to advance the agency’s mission.”

USTR is pleased to announce the 2026 award recipients:

Ambassador’s Award – Recognizes a senior USTR employee who demonstrates excellence, leadership, and tenacity, and whose contributions go significantly beyond the standard and requirements of their role:

  • Daniel Watson, former Assistant United States Trade Representative for the Western Hemisphere

William B. Kelly Award – Recognizes an employee who demonstrates the highest standard of professional excellence in the trade field and demonstrates sustained contributions and leadership in advancing USTR’s goals, an exemplary degree of initiative and creativity, and great respect from peers and superiors:
